claim: Mice exhibited increased locomotion upon acute exposure to cocaine (20 mg/kg, i.p.).
source: Mice exhibited increased locomotion upon acute exposure to cocaine, further increasing following repeated exposure and maintained after abstinence and challenge re-exposure, typical of locomotor sensitization to this intermediate cocaine dose (Figure 1B, F8,312 = 178.9, p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (ANOVA) and reference to Figure 1B showing locomotor data.

claim: Locomotion further increased following repeated cocaine exposure.
source: Mice exhibited increased locomotion upon acute exposure to cocaine, further increasing following repeated exposure and maintained after abstinence and challenge re-exposure, typical of locomotor sensitization to this intermediate cocaine dose (Figure 1B, F8,312 = 178.9, p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1B.

claim: Increased locomotion was maintained after abstinence and challenge re-exposure to cocaine.
source: Mice exhibited increased locomotion upon acute exposure to cocaine, further increasing following repeated exposure and maintained after abstinence and challenge re-exposure, typical of locomotor sensitization to this intermediate cocaine dose (Figure 1B, F8,312 = 178.9, p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 1B.

claim: The observed locomotor response is typical of locomotor sensitization to an intermediate cocaine dose.
source: Mice exhibited increased locomotion upon acute exposure to cocaine, further increasing following repeated exposure and maintained after abstinence and challenge re-exposure, typical of locomotor sensitization to this intermediate cocaine dose (Figure 1B, F8,312 = 178.9, p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cocaine sensitization patterns.

claim: Differentially expressed genes following repeated cocaine exposure and abstinence are associated with categories of neuroplasticity.
source: Baseline shifts in expression of genes associated with categories of neuroplasticity following repeated cocaine exposure and abstinence (see Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2 for description of sectioned regions and RNA-seq QC). Heatmap depicting fold change of differentially expressed genes (normalized to cocaine naive samples and Z-scored per gene), with rows corresponding to individual genes, clustered according to annotation of biological function on Gene Ontology (p<0.05 FDR corrected).
evidence: Supported by Gene Ontology analysis with FDR correction and visualization in Figure 1C.

claim: The dorsal striatum (DS) exhibited the largest number of induced genes following cocaine exposure.
source: The largest number of induced genes, as well as the highest fold induction levels, were found in the DS (Figure 1D,E; refer to Supplementary file 4 for the identities of genes induced in each structure and cocaine condition).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: The dorsal striatum exhibited the highest fold induction levels following cocaine exposure.
source: The largest number of induced genes, as well as the highest fold induction levels, were found in the DS (Figure 1D,E; refer to Supplementary file 4 for the identities of genes induced in each structure and cocaine condition).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Genes induced following different cocaine schedules largely maintain the same temporal structure.
source: This graph reveals aspects of the logic of these inducible transcription programs, whereby (1) genes induced following the different cocaine schedules largely maintain the same temporal structure, i.e., if the peak induction of a given gene was observed at a defined time point in one program, its peak induction time was maintained across other programs
evidence: Based on analysis of temporal gene expression patterns shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Following repeated cocaine exposure, there is substantial dampening of the transcriptional response in the DS.
source: (2) following repeated cocaine exposure, we observe a substantial dampening of the transcriptional response in the DS, which recovers following cocaine challenge, recapitulating a significant proportion of the acute cocaine gene program
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The dampened transcriptional response in the DS recovers following cocaine challenge.
source: (2) following repeated cocaine exposure, we observe a substantial dampening of the transcriptional response in the DS, which recovers following cocaine challenge, recapitulating a significant proportion of the acute cocaine gene program
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: All gene programs largely represent subcomponents of the program induced by acute cocaine in the DS.
source: (3) all gene programs largely represent subcomponents of the program induced by acute cocaine in the DS.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of gene expression programs shown in Figure 1.

claim: The overlap in induced genes between structures stems principally from the immediate component of the transcriptional program (peaking at 1 hr following cocaine).
source: We further visualized the overlap in the identity of genes induced in the different structures using Venn diagrams (Figure 1G), illustrating that the overlap stems principally from the immediate component of the transcriptional program (peaking at 1 hr following cocaine), while transcripts induced at 2 or 4 hr following cocaine diverged between structures.
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Transcripts induced at 2 or 4 hr following cocaine diverged between brain structures.
source: We further visualized the overlap in the identity of genes induced in the different structures using Venn diagrams (Figure 1G), illustrating that the overlap stems principally from the immediate component of the transcriptional program (peaking at 1 hr following cocaine), while transcripts induced at 2 or 4 hr following cocaine diverged between structures.
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Gene clusters enriched at 1 hr time points in the DS are related primarily to transcriptional regulation and synapse-to-nucleus signal transduction.
source: Focusing on the most robust programs, induced in the DS, we found that gene clusters enriched at the 1 hr time points are related primarily to transcriptional regulation and synapse-to-nucleus signal transduction, while clusters related to modification of neural morphology and function were enriched at later time points (Figure 1H; refer to Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Gene clusters related to modification of neural morphology and function were enriched at later time points in the DS.
source: Focusing on the most robust programs, induced in the DS, we found that gene clusters enriched at the 1 hr time points are related primarily to transcriptional regulation and synapse-to-nucleus signal transduction, while clusters related to modification of neural morphology and function were enriched at later time points (Figure 1H; refer to Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Robust induction of Arc, Egr2, Nr4a1, and Fos was observed following acute cocaine exposure.
source: Addressing an overview of induced expression of these IEGs, we observed robust induction of Arc, Egr2, Nr4a1, and Fos following acute cocaine exposure, which was dampened following repeated exposure to cocaine and reinstated following a challenge dose of cocaine, in-line with the results described in Figure 1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: IEG induction was dampened following repeated exposure to cocaine.
source: Addressing an overview of induced expression of these IEGs, we observed robust induction of Arc, Egr2, Nr4a1, and Fos following acute cocaine exposure, which was dampened following repeated exposure to cocaine and reinstated following a challenge dose of cocaine, in-line with the results described in Figure 1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: IEG induction was reinstated following a challenge dose of cocaine.
source: Addressing an overview of induced expression of these IEGs, we observed robust induction of Arc, Egr2, Nr4a1, and Fos following acute cocaine exposure, which was dampened following repeated exposure to cocaine and reinstated following a challenge dose of cocaine, in-line with the results described in Figure 1 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figures 2A-C.

claim: The prominent recruitment of IEG expression in the VLS observed following acute cocaine exposure was dampened drastically after repeated cocaine exposure.
source: The prominent recruitment of IEG expression in the VLS observed following acute cocaine exposure was dampened drastically after repeated cocaine exposure, and re-emerged upon cocaine challenge.
evidence: Based on 2D kernel density estimation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: IEG expression in the VLS re-emerged upon cocaine challenge.
source: The prominent recruitment of IEG expression in the VLS observed following acute cocaine exposure was dampened drastically after repeated cocaine exposure, and re-emerged upon cocaine challenge.
evidence: Based on 2D kernel density estimation analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Dampening of IEG induction in the MS was more modest compared to the VLS.
source: In contrast to the findings in the VLS, dampening of IEG induction in the MS, while evident, was more modest (Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on comparison of spatial patterns shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing Egr2 cells increased to 46 ± 10% after acute cocaine.
source: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing cells of Egr2 increased to 46 ± 10% after acute cocaine, decreased to 21 ± 4% following repeated cocaine, and subsequently increased to 40 ± 11% upon cocaine challenge.
evidence: Quantitative data from smFISH analysis.

claim: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing Egr2 cells decreased to 21 ± 4% following repeated cocaine.
source: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing cells of Egr2 increased to 46 ± 10% after acute cocaine, decreased to 21 ± 4% following repeated cocaine, and subsequently increased to 40 ± 11% upon cocaine challenge.
evidence: Quantitative data from smFISH analysis.

claim: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing Egr2 cells increased to 40 ± 11% upon cocaine challenge.
source: In the VLS, the fraction of robustly expressing cells of Egr2 increased to 46 ± 10% after acute cocaine, decreased to 21 ± 4% following repeated cocaine, and subsequently increased to 40 ± 11% upon cocaine challenge.
evidence: Quantitative data from smFISH analysis.

claim: The expression of different IEGs was highly correlated within individual cells.
source: Notably, the expression of different IEGs was highly correlated within individual cells, defining overlapping populations of neurons responsive to the cocaine experiences studied.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Once recruited by cocaine, neurons committed to co-expression of multiple IEGs to virtually identical levels.
source: Once recruited by cocaine, neurons committed to co-expression of multiple IEGs to virtually identical levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; for detailed statistics, see Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acute exposure to cocaine induces Egr2 expression in both Drd1+ and Drd2+ neurons in the MS.
source: We have previously reported that acute exposure to cocaine induces Egr2 expression in both Drd1+ and Drd2+ neurons in the MS, while more selectively inducing Egr2 expression in Drd1+-neurons in the VLS (Gonzales et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Gonzales et al., 2020).

claim: Acute exposure to cocaine more selectively induces Egr2 expression in Drd1+-neurons in the VLS.
source: We have previously reported that acute exposure to cocaine induces Egr2 expression in both Drd1+ and Drd2+ neurons in the MS, while more selectively inducing Egr2 expression in Drd1+-neurons in the VLS (Gonzales et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Gonzales et al., 2020).

claim: Robust dampening of the induction of Egr2 and Fos in VLS Drd1+ neurons was observed following repeated exposure to cocaine.
source: Extending this analysis to repeated and challenge cocaine exposures and with additional IEGs, we observed robust dampening of the induction of Egr2 and Fos in VLS Drd1+ neurons following repeated exposure to cocaine, while upon cocaine challenge, prominent induction was again evident, especially in Drd1 SPNs.
evidence: Based on smFISH analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Upon cocaine challenge, prominent induction of Egr2 and Fos was again evident in VLS Drd1+ neurons.
source: Extending this analysis to repeated and challenge cocaine exposures and with additional IEGs, we observed robust dampening of the induction of Egr2 and Fos in VLS Drd1+ neurons following repeated exposure to cocaine, while upon cocaine challenge, prominent induction was again evident, especially in Drd1 SPNs.
evidence: Based on smFISH analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the MS, Egr2 and Fos expression maintained consistent correlation to Drd1 and Drd2 expression throughout acute, repeated, and challenge cocaine exposures.
source: In contrast, in the MS, subtle dampening was observed and Egr2 and Fos expression maintained consistent correlation to Drd1 and Drd2 expression throughout acute, repeated, and challenge cocaine exposures (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; for reference of Drd1 and Drd2 levels in MS and VLS, see Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 6 for statistics).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The attenuated transcriptional recruitment in the DS can be attributed to selective dampening of IEG induction, primarily within VLS Drd1+ neurons.
source: Thus, the observed attenuated transcriptional recruitment in the DS can be attributed to selective dampening of IEG induction, primarily within VLS Drd1+ neurons.
evidence: Based on inference from cell-type specific analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of VLS Egr2-expressing neurons impairs cocaine CPP.
source: Chemogenetic inhibition of VLS-Egr2 expressing neurons impairs cocaine CPP.
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Control mice expressing hM4Di and exposed to saline developed CPP following a single conditioning session.
source: In control mice expressing hM4Di and exposed to saline prior to cocaine conditioning sessions, CPP developed following a single conditioning session and was reinforced following additional conditioning sessions (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mice exposed to CNO prior to cocaine conditioning displayed CPP following the initial exposure.
source: The experimental group, which was exposed to CNO (5 mg/kg; i.p.) 30 min prior to cocaine conditioning, also displayed CPP following the initial exposure; however, in this group, the preference decayed with additional conditioning, such that following the third conditioning session, CPP in this group was significantly different from the control group (preference score saline vs. CNO Test3: p<0.05, t = 2, df = 8.6; one-tailed t-test; Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis.

claim: In mice exposed to CNO, the preference decayed with additional conditioning.
source: The experimental group, which was exposed to CNO (5 mg/kg; i.p.) 30 min prior to cocaine conditioning, also displayed CPP following the initial exposure; however, in this group, the preference decayed with additional conditioning, such that following the third conditioning session, CPP in this group was significantly different from the control group (preference score saline vs. CNO Test3: p<0.05, t = 2, df = 8.6; one-tailed t-test; Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3E with statistical analysis.

claim: Both VLS-Egr2hM4Di and VLS-Egr2mCherry groups demonstrated CPP.
source: We found that both groups demonstrated CPP (Figure 3G; paired t-test on % time spent on drug paired side; pVLS-Egr2mCherry < 0.00001, t = −11.362, df = 6; pVLS-Egr2hM4Di < 0.003, t = −4.1232, df = 6).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: Mice in which VLS Egr2+ neurons were inhibited (VLS-Egr2hM4Di) displayed lower preference for the drug paired context compared to control mice (VLS-Egr2mCherry).
source: However, mice in which VLS Egr2+ neurons were inhibited (VLS-Egr2hM4Di) displayed lower preference for the drug paired context (preference score) compared to control mice (VLS-Egr2mCherry) (Figure 3G; p<0.05, t = 1.95, df = 9.4, one-tailed t-test).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in locomotion were observed between VLS-Egr2hM4Di and VLS-Egr2mCherry groups on conditioning or test days.
source: Importantly, no differences in locomotion were observed between groups on conditioning or test days (p=0.93, F4,48 = 0.19, ANOVA; Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Based on locomotor data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C with statistical analysis.

claim: VLS Egr2+-expressing neurons contribute to the development of cocaine-seeking behavior.
source: We therefore conclude that VLS Egr2+-expressing neurons contribute to the development of cocaine-seeking behavior, with no obvious impact on locomotor aspects of cocaine-driven behavior.
evidence: Based on inference from chemogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: VLS Egr2+-expressing neurons have no obvious impact on locomotor aspects of cocaine-driven behavior.
source: We therefore conclude that VLS Egr2+-expressing neurons contribute to the development of cocaine-seeking behavior, with no obvious impact on locomotor aspects of cocaine-driven behavior.
evidence: Based on inference from chemogenetic inhibition experiments and locomotor data.

claim: Both VLSGFP and VLSDNEgr2 groups of mice developed CPP.
source: Comparing the development of cocaine CPP, we found that both groups of mice developed CPP (Figure 3I, paired t-test on % time spent on drug paired side; pVLS-GFP <0.001, t = −4.9782, df = 7; pVLS-DNEgr2 <0.05, t = −2.2199, df = 7).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis.

claim: VLSDNEgr2 mice developed lower CPP than VLSGFP mice.
source: However, VLSDNEgr2 developed lower CPP than VLSGFP mice (Figure 3I, p<0.05, t = 2.36, df = 14, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Based on behavioral data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis.

claim: No differences in locomotion were observed between VLSGFP and VLSDNEgr2 groups.
source: No differences in locomotion were observed between the groups of mice (p=0.7, F4,56 = 0.54, ANOVA; Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Based on locomotor data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C with statistical analysis.

claim: Induction of the IEG Egr2 in the ventrolateral striatum is required for the development of cocaine seeking.
source: These results assign a functional role to Egr2 induction, primarily within VLS Drd1+ neurons, in the development of conditioned-place preference to cocaine.
evidence: Based on inference from DN-Egr2 experiments.

claim: In the VLS, overexpression of DN-Egr2 resulted in blunted Arc and Nr4a1 expression.
source: In the VLS, we observed the anticipated overexpression of Egr2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, p(Egr2)<0.05, t = −5.3616, df = 2; two-tailed t-test, reflecting exogenous expression of the mutant gene), as well as blunted Arc and Nr4a1 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 4D, p(Arc)<0.01, t = 6, df = 2.8; p(Nr4a1)<0.005, t = 6.2, df = 3.8; two-tailed t-test).
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D with statistical analysis.

claim: No clear differences in gene expression were observed between VLSGFP and VLSDNEgr2 groups within structures other than the VLS.
source: We did not observe any clear differences in gene expression between groups within other structures, demonstrating the localized effect of our viral manipulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E–G).
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E-G.

claim: Inducible transcriptional complexes involving Egr2 are functional in facilitating drug-induced maladaptive plasticity.
source: These results demonstrate a role for cocaine-induced expression of Egr2 in the VLS in supporting the development of cocaine-seeking and suggest that inducible transcriptional complexes involving Egr2 are functional in facilitating drug-induced maladaptive plasticity.
evidence: Based on inference from DN-Egr2 experiments and gene expression analysis.

claim: Drugs of abuse such as cocaine act on key brain circuits, modifying and biasing the future behavior of an individual toward increased drug seeking.
source: Drugs of abuse such as cocaine are known to act on key brain circuits, modifying and biasing the future behavior of an individual toward increased drug seeking.
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The striatum is a major hub of plasticity during cocaine sensitization.
source: We highlight the striatum as a major hub of plasticity, within which we identify differential transcriptional recruitment of neuronal ensembles by cocaine, dependent on striatal subdomain, identity of projection neurons and the history of cocaine exposure.
evidence: Based on comprehensive transcriptional analysis presented in the study.

claim: Egr2-expressing SPNs in the VLS support drug-seeking behavior.
source: Finally, we focus on a prominent cocaine-sensitive IEG, Egr2, and show that Egr2-expressing SPNs in the VLS, and the expression of Egr2 within them, support drug-seeking behavior.
evidence: Based on chemogenetic and DN-Egr2 experiments.

claim: Expression of Egr2 within VLS SPNs supports drug-seeking behavior.
source: Finally, we focus on a prominent cocaine-sensitive IEG, Egr2, and show that Egr2-expressing SPNs in the VLS, and the expression of Egr2 within them, support drug-seeking behavior.
evidence: Based on DN-Egr2 experiments.

claim: Repeated exposure to cocaine produces long-lasting functional changes in the reward circuit.
source: Repeated exposure to cocaine, as well as abstinence, produces long-lasting functional changes in the reward circuit to drive the maladaptive modification of reinforced behavior (Dong and Nestler, 2014; Everitt, 2014; Gremel and Lovinger, 2017; Hyman et al., 2006; Kelley, 2004; Lüscher, 2016; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Nestler, 2013; Russo and Nestler, 2013; Salery et al., 2020; Volkow and Morales, 2015; Wolf, 2016; Zahm et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Abstinence from cocaine produces long-lasting functional changes in the reward circuit.
source: Repeated exposure to cocaine, as well as abstinence, produces long-lasting functional changes in the reward circuit to drive the maladaptive modification of reinforced behavior (Dong and Nestler, 2014; Everitt, 2014; Gremel and Lovinger, 2017; Hyman et al., 2006; Kelley, 2004; Lüscher, 2016; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Nestler, 2013; Russo and Nestler, 2013; Salery et al., 2020; Volkow and Morales, 2015; Wolf, 2016; Zahm et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cocaine-induced modifications in gene expression support the imprinting of potentially lifelong alterations in behavior.
source: The imprinting of such potentially lifelong alterations in behavior driven by drug experience is supported by cocaine-induced modifications in gene expression (McClung and Nestler, 2008; Nestler, 2002; Nestler and Lüscher, 2019; Salery et al., 2020; Steiner, 2016; Steiner and Van Waes, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Myelin genes (Plp1, Mobp, Mbp, Mal, Pllp) were downregulated across all structures studied following repeated cocaine exposure.
source: Myelin genes (Plp1, Mobp, Mbp, Mal, Pllp) were downregulated across all structures studied (LCtx, Amy, NAc, DS, LH), initially following repeated cocaine exposure, and further following abstinence, across all experimental mice.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of baseline transcription.

claim: Myelin genes were further downregulated following abstinence from cocaine.
source: Myelin genes (Plp1, Mobp, Mbp, Mal, Pllp) were downregulated across all structures studied (LCtx, Amy, NAc, DS, LH), initially following repeated cocaine exposure, and further following abstinence, across all experimental mice.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of baseline transcription.

claim: Genes associated with proteostasis (e.g., chaperones such as members of the CCT, Hsp40, Hsp70, and Hsp90 complexes) were upregulated in concert across structures following cocaine abstinence.
source: Conversely, genes associated with proteostasis (e.g., chaperones such as members of the CCT, Hsp40, Hsp70, and Hsp90 complexes) were upregulated in concert across structures following cocaine abstinence.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of baseline transcription.

claim: Similar changes in myelin genes have been described in both human and rodent studies.
source: Notably, similar changes in myelin genes and genes associated with proteostasis have been described in both human and rodent studies (Albertson et al., 2004; Bannon et al., 2014; García-Fuster et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2012; Kovalevich et al., 2012; Lull et al., 2008; Narayana et al., 2014), but their functional implications remain unknown.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Similar changes in genes associated with proteostasis have been described in both human and rodent studies.
source: Notably, similar changes in myelin genes and genes associated with proteostasis have been described in both human and rodent studies (Albertson et al., 2004; Bannon et al., 2014; García-Fuster et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2012; Kovalevich et al., 2012; Lull et al., 2008; Narayana et al., 2014), but their functional implications remain unknown.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The functional implications of changes in myelin genes and proteostasis genes remain unknown.
source: Notably, similar changes in myelin genes and genes associated with proteostasis have been described in both human and rodent studies (Albertson et al., 2004; Bannon et al., 2014; García-Fuster et al., 2012; Johnson et al., 2012; Kovalevich et al., 2012; Lull et al., 2008; Narayana et al., 2014), but their functional implications remain unknown.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap.

claim: IEG expression is the substrate for long-term modulations supporting memory formation.
source: IEG expression is well accepted to be the substrate for long-term modulations supporting memory formation (Alberini, 2009; Alberini and Kandel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The immediate-early transcriptional programs induced across tissues largely consisted of subcomponents of DS programs.
source: Furthermore, the immediate-early transcriptional programs induced across other tissues largely consisted of subcomponents of DS programs.
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of gene expression programs.

claim: The core transcriptome predominantly corresponds to signaling molecules and transcriptional regulators.
source: This core component predominantly corresponds to signaling molecules and transcriptional regulators (the genes common across most programs are Arc, Arl4d, Btg2, Ddit4, Dusp1, Egr2, Egr4, Fos, Fosb, Junb, Nr4a1, Per1, and Tiparp), likely responsible for transforming inducing signals into instructions for implementation of appropriate synaptic, cellular, and circuit-specific plasticity mechanisms by 'effector' genes.
evidence: Based on analysis of commonly induced genes.

claim: Downstream effector genes are induced in a secondary wave of transcription, corresponding to the significantly diversified gene response at 2–4 hr following cocaine.
source: These downstream effector genes are induced in a secondary wave of transcription, corresponding to the significantly diversified gene response at 2–4 hr following cocaine (Amit et al., 2007; Clayton et al., 2020; Gray and Spiegel, 2019; Hrvatin et al., 2018; Mukherjee et al., 2018; Tyssowski et al., 2018; Yap and Greenberg, 2018).
evidence: Based on temporal analysis of gene expression supported by citations.

claim: Co-expression of genes overlapping with the putative 'core transcriptome' in the NAc increased SPN excitability and enhanced the development of cocaine sensitization.
source: Interestingly, a recent landmark study (Savell et al., 2020) utilized a multiplexed CRISPR strategy to drive co-expression of genes overlapping with many of the components of the putative 'core transcriptome' (Btg2, Egr2, Egr4, Fos, FosB, JunB, and Nr4a1) in the NAc and found that this manipulation increased SPN excitability and enhanced the development of cocaine sensitization.
evidence: Supported by citation to Savell et al., 2020.

claim: The MS is defined as the 'associative striatum' and is associated with goal-directed behaviors.
source: The MS is defined as the 'associative striatum' and is associated with goal-directed behaviors, as well as defining the vigor of locomotor actions (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Balleine and Ostlund, 2007; Kravitz et al., 2010; Lipton et al., 2019; Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The MS is associated with defining the vigor of locomotor actions.
source: The MS is defined as the 'associative striatum' and is associated with goal-directed behaviors, as well as defining the vigor of locomotor actions (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Balleine and Ostlund, 2007; Kravitz et al., 2010; Lipton et al., 2019; Nonomura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Cocaine-driven locomotor sensitization may be mediated by the balanced and largely maintained transcriptional induction within Drd1/Drd2 SPNs in the MS.
source: We propose that the cocaine-driven locomotor sensitization may be mediated by the balanced and largely maintained transcriptional induction within Drd1/Drd2 SPNs in the MS.
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on data.

claim: The lateral 'sensori-motor' striatum is strongly associated with habit formation and compulsive drug seeking.
source: The lateral 'sensori-motor' striatum is strongly associated with habit formation and compulsive drug seeking (Lipton et al., 2019; Yin et al., 2004; Zapata et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The VLS receives selective sensorimotor afferents mapped to upper limb and orofacial cortical regions.
source: Moreover, the VLS receives selective sensorimotor afferents mapped to upper limb and orofacial cortical regions.
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Behavioral stereotypies, primarily upper limb and orofacial, arise upon high-dose psychostimulant exposure.
source: Interestingly, behavioral stereotypies, primarily upper limb and orofacial, arise upon high-dose psychostimulant exposure (Karler et al., 1994; Murray et al., 2015; Schlussman et al., 2003), and orofacial stereotypies have been induced following selective infusion of psychostimulants to the VLS (Baker et al., 1998; Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Rebec et al., 1997; White et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Orofacial stereotypies have been induced following selective infusion of psychostimulants to the VLS.
source: Interestingly, behavioral stereotypies, primarily upper limb and orofacial, arise upon high-dose psychostimulant exposure (Karler et al., 1994; Murray et al., 2015; Schlussman et al., 2003), and orofacial stereotypies have been induced following selective infusion of psychostimulants to the VLS (Baker et al., 1998; Delfs and Kelley, 1990; Rebec et al., 1997; White et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Recruitment of plasticity mechanisms within VLS Drd1+ neurons may support the increased propensity to engage in orofacial stereotypies.
source: It is intriguing to consider the possibility that recruitment of plasticity mechanisms within VLS Drd1+ neurons supports the increased propensity to engage in orofacial stereotypies, while the subsequent dampening of cocaine-induced transcription within these neurons may indicate the 'canalization' of this limited action repertoire, at the expense of a broader behavioral repertoire.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: The subsequent dampening of cocaine-induced transcription within VLS Drd1+ neurons may indicate the 'canalization' of a limited action repertoire.
source: It is intriguing to consider the possibility that recruitment of plasticity mechanisms within VLS Drd1+ neurons supports the increased propensity to engage in orofacial stereotypies, while the subsequent dampening of cocaine-induced transcription within these neurons may indicate the 'canalization' of this limited action repertoire, at the expense of a broader behavioral repertoire.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Infusion of psychostimulants into the VLS has been shown to promote operant reinforcement and conditioned-place preference.
source: Infusion of psychostimulants into the VLS has also been shown to promote operant reinforcement and conditioned-place preference, implicating it in reward and reinforcement (Baker et al., 1998; Kelley and Delfs, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: This study provides the first functional implication of the VLS in cocaine seeking.
source: Thus, to our knowledge, we provide the first functional implication of the VLS in cocaine seeking.
evidence: Authors' claim of novelty based on their experimental results.

claim: The development and execution of drug-seeking behavior is heavily context dependent.
source: The development and execution of drug-seeking behavior is heavily context dependent (Calipari et al., 2016; Crombag et al., 2002; Crombag et al., 2008; Crombag and Shaham, 2002; Cruz et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2006; Rubio et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The dampening of sensorimotor VLS IEG induction following repeated cocaine could serve to 'cement' the initial context association.
